newsitem.title: USA: GM emerging from UAW battles with fewer workers.
newsitem.headline: GM emerging from UAW battles with fewer workers.

text.p: It's a scenario all too familiar to General Motors Corp. in recent years -- workers at a key parts plant strike over demands for more jobs and assembly plants grind to a halt, sending ripples through the U.S. economy.

The drama started again this week when 2,800 United Auto Workers members struck a Warren, Mich., plant that makes transmissions, wheels and suspension parts. Six GM assembly lines were silent Friday and 20 more could be idled in the next two weeks.
So goes the rocky relationship between the world's largest automaker and the most powerful U.S. labor union. Who's winning this war of wills?

Although GM ends every local strike by adding jobs to the plant in question, analysts say the settlements are only minor setbacks to its long-term plans to shrink its work force through attrition and pare costs to competitive levels.
By taking advantage of massive retirements of workers hired in the 1960s, the auto giant remains on track to meet eliminate 30,000 jobs over the next three years.
GM ended the second quarter with 227,000 U.S. hourly workers, down from 244,000 a year earlier -- a decline that has led to some of the current tension at individual plants.

"They have not abandoned the basic model that uses attrition to downsize their labor force," said David Cole, director of the University of Michigan's Office for the Study of Automotive Transportation.
"I think they will still be able to shed 30,000 to 35,000 people over a three-year period," Cole added.
To end a festering, three-month walkout at truck facilities in Pontiac, Mich., last week, GM agreed to add 557 new jobs, not much below the UAW's demand for 600 new jobs.
But analysts note that the pact won't prevent GM from reducing the work force at the plant when it begins producing a new, easier-to-build pickup truck there next year.
In addition, not all of the workers promised to each plant are new hires. In its vast manufacturing base in Michigan, GM has the ability to shift workers to plants where they are needed.
With a war chest of $14.9 billion in cash and stock, GM has shown its resolve, as it did during the 85-day Pontiac strike, which cost workers some $15,000 in lost wages.

Last year, GM endured a 17-day strike at two Dayton, Ohio, brake plants that forced the shutdown of 26 assembly plants at a cost of $900 million in lost profits. Despite the cost, investors have enthusiastically supported GM's tough stance and will continue to do so, analysts say.
GM shares, though off $1.44 at $56.875 on the New York Stock Exchange Friday, have been hovering near their 52-week high of $63.75.
Furman Selz Inc. auto analyst Maryann Keller said would be more upset if GM caved in and gave up more of its recent productivity gains.

"From a market standpoint, it's a non-event," she said of the strikes. "At the end of the day, GM seems to resolve these conflicts with acceptable financial penalties. As long as that's the case, investors will support them."

The conflicts are likely to continue for another few months -- GM has about 10 locals that are still trying to negotiate new local labor contracts, including the same Dayton brake plants that went on strike last year.
Others include a transmission plant in Ypsilanti, Mich., and the GM's Cadillac plant in Hamtramck, Mich.
And as Ford Motor Co., Chrysler Corp. and Japanese automakers work feverishly to cut their costs further, GM could remain a step behind, which could lead to future disputes with the UAW.
"The guy down the street is not going to be letting up, either. Everybody is going to be driving for reductions in total assembled cost."
Salt Lake City Chevrolet dealer Gerald Seiner said he fully supports GM's drive to slash its costs.
"I can't sell cars and trucks that are priced higher than our competition," he said. "We have to have value in our products. Otherwise, we won't be here long-term."
